So I accidentally picked up a big handfull of Game of Malkavs on ebay
for, like, nothing (10 for a buck or something). As a result I put
together a deck to reliably play Game of Malkav (a G1/2 weenie obf/aus
deck revolving around the 4x3 caps with aus/obf and 2 each of Zoe and
Victoria) that is using 4 or 5 of them for multiple plays a game.

So I'm trying to figure out how to best utilize Game of Malkav in a way
that limits the randomosity of it (Game of Malkav is the one where
everyone puts between 1-5 pool in their hands, I put 1-6 pool in my
hand, we all reveal, and if anyone picks exactly 1 less than you, you
lose that much pool, otherwise you gain that much pool). So the basic
Game of Malkav theory likely goes like this:

-Somone is bound to pick 1, as you can't lose if you pick 1.
-Because somone is picking 1, no one will pick 2.
-Because no one will pick 2, someone is gonna pick 3. Which makes 4
right out, but 5 probably pretty good, meaning 6 is probably not really
a good idea either.

So that is likely the basic concept of the game. But then you can
second and third guess people ("I'm gonna pick 2 just to screw all the
people who pick 3!") Which goes mad.

So assuming I'm playing Game of Malkav, and not doing so specifically
to piss everyone off, do I:

A) Pick 1.
B) Pick some other number that isn't 1.
C) Pick a random number by rolling a die.

Clearly, if I play the card more than once, I gotta do something
different every time. Or something. Any ideas?

Then--is there a way to make the card less random, like you can with
the other one ("You! Pick 4! I call you have, uh, 2!")? I don't think
there really is, as if you try and announce something, someone will
clearly screw with everyone ("Hey! Everyone pick 5 pool so we all gain
5 pool!" "I picked 4...")

-Peter

Not really important for most situations, but if you play Game of Malkav with
just one other Methuselah remaining, then you can treat it as a zero-sum game
(although it's not really zero-sum; you have to fudge and treat the "score" as
the difference in pool gain (or loss) -- so the numbers only work if both
players have "sufficient" pool) But anyway...

If there are only 2p and the game is treated as a zero-sum game with a score
based only on the net pool gain compared to your opponent, the optimal strategy
for the Methuselah who played the GoM is:
00.00% : 1
44.99% : 2
14.27% : 3
31.96% : 4
00.00% : 5
08.78% : 6

For the opponent, the optimal strategy is:
00.00% : 1
25.19% : 2
28.07% : 3
27.44% : 4
19.30% : 5

The expected (average) outcome if both players play optimally is a 0.5517 net
gain for the Methuselah who played the GoM.

Note that neither player should ever choose 1. Even though this is the "safe"
choice, it usually means a loss when considered against what the other player
gains, so much so that it is never a choice in "optimal" play (optimal with the
caveats above).

a lot of other options these days. Then you also need a player who's
intelligent enough to use the card well. And you need a player who's
got some spare master slots in his deck, that aren't being used by all
the other master cards he might include - Blood Doll, The Barrens,

On average, you give more to your allies than to your enemies. My
allies always get 4. My enemies might get between 1 and 4, but also
might lose between 1 and 4, depending on a lot of things.

In the worst case scenario, my allies get +4 and so do my enemies. In
the best case scenario, my allies get +4 and my enemies get -4, and I
also get +4. On average, my allies are doing better than my enemies.

Why is being able to do something that's potentially significantly more
beneficial to my allies than my enemies always poor play? When I want
to keep someone in the game so I can pass my vote with their votes and
oust my prey, why is giving them +4 pool to keep them out of range of
Smiling Jack poor play? Or to keep them out of range of a bleed oust?
Or to prevent a play of Foreshadowing Destruction?

A potentially interesting option would be to see how greedy players get,
and then use the extra pool they have to your advantage in a Parity
Shift - whilst *also* helping your allies. If my enemies get +3 or 4
pool, I take it off them. If they get +1 or 2 pool, that's a
significant gain for my allies (relatively), and I'll kill them anyway.
The Malkavians aren't short of good ways of passing a vote these days.
Even in Group 1/2, you have a couple of Princes with AUS. Go to Group
3, and you have Quentin King III with AUS/pre, which is pretty fearsome,
and you can still nick Greger (Prince, AUS) from Group 2, and include
Rachel Brandywine or Maris Streck too, if you like that sort of thing -
Rachel is particularly popular. Lazarus James lacks a title, but
AUS/PRE means he might be a worthwhile include. Or you might like to
include Fleurdumal (Toreador), for his keen sense of AUS/DEM/PRE, though
the lack of Obf might be a tad too annoying in a mostly Malk deck.

Combine with normal pool control options - Secret Horde, for example,
spare vampires to move pool onto, permanent Blood Dolls already in play
etc. Now you have an interesting little pool manipulation scheme going
on.

>> but not with Malkavian Prank?
>
>There is no risk with Anarchist Uprising. You know how much pool
>everyone will have after the vote. You don't know how much pool
>everyone will have after a Prank. Why don't you see the difference?

Sure there's risk with Anarchist Uprising. I play it to help myself,
but at the same time there's my cross-table buddy teetering on the edge
of being ousted, because I've just knocked him down from 5 pool (where
he could probably survive) to 2 pool (where he might well not be able
to).

Will that mean my prey eats my buddy (my grand-prey) before I can eat my
prey? That's a calculated risk I have to take. It's a different risk,
but it's still a risk. If risks are bad, ban all play that brings other
players to the brink of disaster.

Many, many cards and plays on the table involve calculated risks. If I
bring out a vampire, will it help me? Quite probably. Will it mean I
get ousted due to having three less pool? Who can say. Will Malkavian
Game help me by keeping my allies in play? Quite possibly. Will it
help my enemies? Who can say.

Why are some calculated risks fine, but others aren't?

Also, I know how much pool any allies will have after the Prank.
Because I'm letting them have it. Then I can work out what my enemies
*might* get.

You can also work out what the worst possible scenario is, and still
decide it's worth it. My grand-prey survives for another turn (for
example), and even if my prey has 4 more pool, it's fine, I can still
get him - because my grand-prey is still on the table with some votes,
or whatever. And I can limit my prey's gain to 3 pool also, by guessing
4 - if he's lower, he's got at most 3, if he's guessed 4, I'm quids in.
So I offer to keep my grand-prey in if he passes my votes, or saves my
vampire from a Blood Hunt, or something. Then I oust my prey with that
support. And I offer to help my grand-prey oust his prey. Then we
fight it out for the remaining VPs.

Please explain where the non-play-to-win play was, and why I shouldn't
be allowed to help my grand-prey in this scenario.

to not oust him, but in all likelyhood self preservation will win out
over arbitrarily imposed "play to win" guidelines--if I play Malkavian
Prank when my grand prey is at 1 pool, why would I *not* arrange to
give him 4 pool? Either 'cause I want him dead (for some reason or
another, so if I want him dead, I likely want him dead as it helps my
chance of winning, thus playing to win) or 'cause I'm playing stupid
(which isn't the fault of the card).

*All* cards are subject to the "play to win" rule. As Game of Malkav
(which is much more random than Malkavian Prank, but you keep switching
back and forth between the two in discussion) is random, but on the
average more helpful than not, just like any other card, when you play
it, you should be playing it in hopes that it will help you win (as
otherwise, you are just playing stupid, and again, you can play stupid
with any card: "I'm a crazy Malkavian! I'm gonna bleed you arbitrarily
cross table for 4 with this here Kindred Spirits! 'Cause I rolled a die
and picked you! Woo!")

> me in a tournament i would call a judge.

ousted by KRC, it was the result of "I think you are going to sweep the
table if I don't kill you now, even though it will only strengthen my
prey..." Very easily an arguable "I'm playing to win" decision,
regardless of whether or not the person doing it actually ends up
winning--they think what they are doing is going to help them win, so
they are playing to win. In the other example, where I was killed by
cross table Anarchist Uprising collateral damage, I'm sure thay guy
thought he was doing the best thing at the time too--he was hurting his
prey, and he probably thought that he was going to be able to oust him
before he ousted me, even though I was getting hurt more by the AU then

even though it turned out to not be.
